ch15.essay:
Chowder is the book's exhale. We have just come through a chapel full of cenotaphs, a sermon about Jonah, a night in bed with a cannibal, and a leaky schooner—and now Melville sits us down and feeds us. I find I trust a writer more when he can be this happy about a bowl of soup. The recipe paragraph ("small juicy clams, scarcely bigger than hazel nuts") is written with the same attention he will later give to the whale's skeleton, and that is the point: the same eye that will be terrified by the whiteness of the whale can also be delighted by pounded ship biscuit.

But notice the chapter's first gesture isn't warmth. It's Ishmael staring at a top-mast that looks like a gallows, counting the two remaining horns, "one for Queequeg, and one for me." He is doing what he did with the Coffin at the Spouter-Inn: reading omens into furniture. Then Mrs. Hussey says "Clam or Cod?" and the omen collapses into a comedy of miscommunication. That is the book's rhythm in miniature—dread, then a joke, then a meal.

The thing I keep coming back to is the harpoon rule. Young Stiggs, back from an "unfort'nt v'y'ge" with only three barrels of oil, was found dead with his harpoon in his side. Mrs. Hussey turns a suicide into a house policy about weapons in bedrooms, the way institutions always convert grief into procedure. And it sets up the next chapter's locked-door panic almost too neatly. Melville is planting; I only see it on the second read.

annotations.quote: A sort of crick was in my neck as I gazed up to the two remaining horns; yes, _two_ of them, one for Queequeg, and one for me.
annotations.note: Ishmael cannot look at any object without reading his own death into it. What's funny is how bodily it is—a crick in the neck from staring up at a gallows. The book will keep asking whether omens are real or just what a nervous mind does with a top-mast.

annotations.quote: Oh, sweet friends! hearken to me.
annotations.note: The tone of a preacher, borrowed for a chowder recipe. Father Mapple used almost this register two chapters ago about Jonah. Melville is telling you, gently, that the sacred and the delicious run on the same voltage in this book.

annotations.quote: Chowder for breakfast, and chowder for dinner, and chowder for supper, till you began to look for fish-bones coming through your clothes.
annotations.note: A whole island's economy has soaked into its milk. It's a joke, but it's also the first description in the book of what living entirely inside one industry does to a person—which is what the Pequod will be.

annotations.quote: was found dead in my first floor back, with his harpoon in his side; ever since then I allow no boarders to take sich dangerous weepons in their rooms at night.
annotations.note: A suicide reduced to a house rule, delivered in the same breath as 'clam or cod for breakfast.' I find that more chilling than a solemn treatment would be. Also: it is the seed of the whole next chapter.

links.why: The first inn and its practical joke; Mrs. Hussey is the Spouter-Inn's sequel.
Queequeg's Ramadan begins the next morning in this same inn.

ch16.essay:
This is the chapter where the book's machinery gets bolted together, and what surprises me every time is how much of the bolting is done as comedy. Look at the mechanism of the first paragraph. Yojo, Queequeg's little black god, insists that Ishmael choose the ship alone—so that the vessel fate has already picked will be found "for all the world as though it had turned out by chance." That subordinate clause is doing an enormous amount of work. It tells you, in the voice of a man reporting a friend's superstition, that the novel you are reading runs on a theory of providence in which free choice is real *as an experience* and unreal as a cause. Ishmael will feel he chose the Pequod; the text has already chosen it for him. This is exactly the knot the book ties more solemnly later—[[ch47:chance, free will, and necessity|the three-stranded loom of the Mat-Maker]], Ahab's "[[ch132:Is Ahab, Ahab|Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm?]]"—but here it arrives as a joke about a wooden idol, and I think that is the right place for a first-time reader to meet it: lightly, before it can frighten you.

The ship herself gets the chapter's best writing, and the writing is a lesson in how Melville makes objects moral. Notice the sequence of comparisons: a French grenadier, the three kings of Cologne, the flagstone where Becket bled, an Ethiopian emperor. Every simile makes the Pequod older and more sacred than a small whaler has any right to be, and then the paragraph turns: "She was a thing of trophies. A cannibal of a craft, tricking herself forth in the chased bones of her enemies." The bulwarks are pinned with sperm-whale teeth "like one continuous jaw"; the tiller is carved from the lower jaw of "her hereditary foe." What the description is really saying is that the ship is made of the thing it hunts. Twelve chapters ago Ishmael was afraid to sleep beside a cannibal. Now the word has migrated onto the Christian, commercial vessel, and it will keep migrating—onto the crew, onto the economy, onto the reader—until it is clear that Queequeg was never the cannibal in this book. And then the throwaway law: "A noble craft, but somehow a most melancholy! All noble things are touched with that." Melville drops a universal claim about nobility inside a piece of ship-description, as if it cost nothing. It is the first statement of the rule Ahab will embody.

Then the fighting Quakers, and the lay negotiation, which I read as the funniest scene in the first quarter of the book and also the most quietly damning. Bildad is reading "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth" at the very moment he is offering Ishmael the seven hundred and seventy-seventh *lay*: the pun is Melville's, and the theology is exact—the man quoting the verse has spent his life laying up treasure, and the verse he cannot finish is the one that condemns him. Then he invokes "widows and orphans" as the reason to underpay a sailor. That is capital speaking in scripture's voice, and what I admire is that Melville refuses to sneer. He is genuinely fascinated that Bildad's mind holds "a sworn foe to human bloodshed" and "tuns upon tuns of leviathan gore" in the same drab waistcoat, and his verdict—"This world pays dividends"—is not a punchline so much as a diagnosis. A first-time reader may take Peleg for the honest one because he swears; watch instead how the two men need each other, and how the "squall" of their quarrel blows over into perfect cooperation. They are one institution with two faces.

And then, buried in the middle of a paragraph about Bildad, a passage that is not about Bildad at all. Melville stops to describe a man with "a globular brain and a ponderous heart," who has thought "untraditionally and independently" under strange constellations and learned "a bold and nervous lofty language"—"a mighty pageant creature, formed for noble tragedies." Then: "all mortal greatness is but disease." We are twelve chapters from meeting [[ch28|Ahab]], and this is his overture, slipped into a chapter about paperwork and disguised as a digression Melville immediately retracts ("But, as yet we have not to do with such an one"). It is worth reading twice, because it states the book's most unsettling idea about its hero—that his morbidness is not a flaw in his greatness but its condition—before you have any reason to resist it.

Peleg's closing speech is where the chapter finally lets you feel something. "He's a grand, ungodly, god-like man"—a contradiction held in one breath, and it will turn out to be precise. Peleg tells Ishmael about the wife, "a sweet, resigned girl," and the child, and ends: "stricken, blasted, if he be, Ahab has his humanities!" Everything he says is true and none of it will matter, and Melville has arranged for the plea to come from a blusterer so that it lands harder than piety could. When Ahab himself finally speaks of that girl, forty years later in ship-time and a hundred chapters later in ours, he will say he [[ch132:widowed that poor girl|widowed her by marrying her]]. Hold Peleg's version next to that one; the distance between them is the book.

annotations.quote: for all the world as though it had turned out by chance
annotations.note: Yojo's plan is that Ishmael's free choice will feel free while being fated. It is a comic sentence, but it is the book's whole stance on predestination stated in advance: the loom weaves, and you think you are holding the shuttle. Keep this clause in mind when you reach [[ch47:chance, free will, and necessity|the Mat-Maker]], where the same idea is given its solemn form.

annotations.quote: _Pequod_, you will no doubt remember, was the name of a celebrated tribe of Massachusetts Indians; now extinct as the ancient Medes.
annotations.note: The ship is named for a people who were massacred. 'You will no doubt remember' is Ishmael's dry way of noting that nobody remembers. A ship named for the exterminated, crewed by a Gay Head Indian, hunting a species toward extinction—Melville does not underline it, and he does not need to. The question of whether the whale can be wiped out gets its own chapter much later, [[ch105]].

annotations.quote: A cannibal of a craft, tricking herself forth in the chased bones of her enemies.
annotations.note: Twelve chapters ago Ishmael was afraid of sleeping next to a cannibal ([[ch3]], [[ch4]]). Now the ship itself is one, dressed in the bones of what it eats, with a tiller carved from a whale's jaw. The word keeps migrating from the 'savage' to everything Christian and commercial around him, and by the end you will have to ask who in this book actually eats whom.

annotations.quote: A noble craft, but somehow a most melancholy! All noble things are touched with that.
annotations.note: A universal law tossed off inside a ship description. I do not know whether it is true of the world, but the book behaves as though it is—every noble thing in it, Ahab most of all, is shadowed. This is the first, gentlest statement of the rule that [[ch16:all mortal greatness is but disease|the Bildad paragraph]] will make harsh a few pages on.

annotations.quote: Can’t ye see the world where you stand?
annotations.note: Peleg's test is brutal and true. Ishmael says he wants to see the world; Peleg sends him to look over the bow and it is nothing but water and a squall. That is what he is signing up for: three years of the same nothing, which the book will insist is either emptiness or everything. Compare Ishmael's own later account of what the sea's blankness does to a mind in [[ch35:Descartian vortices|The Mast-Head]].

annotations.quote: Be sure of this, O young ambition, all mortal greatness is but disease.
annotations.note: This is not about Bildad, the man supposedly being described. Melville interrupts himself to prophesy Ahab, whom we will not see for twelve more chapters, and then retracts the digression as if embarrassed by it. Read it twice: he calls the 'half wilful overruling morbidness' a qualification for greatness, not a flaw in it. When Ahab appears in [[ch28]] 'with a crucifixion in his face,' this is the sentence that has already explained him.

annotations.quote: a man’s religion is one thing, and this practical world quite another. This world pays dividends.
annotations.note: The most economical indictment of comfortable piety I know. Bildad is a sworn foe of bloodshed who has spilled 'tuns upon tuns of leviathan gore,' and the reconciliation is simply: dividends. Melville is not sneering exactly—he seems fascinated that it works. The ship's whole economy of lays and shares is the same reconciliation scaled up; see how Ishmael describes it as a form of slavery he does not mind in [[ch1]].

annotations.quote: “_Lay_ not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth—”
annotations.note: Bildad is reading the one verse in scripture that puns on the word he is about to use to cheat Ishmael. The comedy is perfect and the theology exact: the man quoting it has laid up treasures on earth his whole life, and the verse he keeps failing to finish is the one that condemns him.

annotations.quote: we may be taking the bread from those widows and those orphans.
annotations.note: Widows and orphans as the reason to underpay a sailor. It is a real argument—those annuitants do own 'a nail or two in the ship'—and that is what makes it awful: Bildad is not lying, he is describing how capital launders itself through the vulnerable. The book will end on a real orphan, in the [[epilogue:another orphan|Epilogue]], and I cannot read this line without hearing that one.

annotations.quote: He’s a grand, ungodly, god-like man, Captain Ahab
annotations.note: Peleg's phrase is the book's first attempt to describe Ahab and it is a contradiction held in one breath. 'Ungodly, god-like' will turn out to be precise: a man who defies God by trying to be one. Ahab's own version of this comes in [[ch119:speechless, placeless power|The Candles]], where he tells the lightning that he worships it by defying it.

annotations.quote: by that sweet girl that old man has a child: hold ye then there can be any utter, hopeless harm in Ahab?
annotations.note: Peleg's argument is that a man with a young wife and a child cannot be hopeless. The book will test that argument to destruction. In [[ch132:widowed that poor girl|The Symphony]] Ahab himself says he widowed the girl by marrying her, and Starbuck's last appeal to him is exactly this one—the wife, the child—and it fails.

annotations.quote: stricken, blasted, if he be, Ahab has his humanities!
annotations.note: A wife, a child, a moody good man who will come round. Everything Peleg says here is true and none of it will matter. It is the last defense of Ahab offered by someone who loves him, before we meet him and it becomes impossible either to defend him or to look away.

links.why: The man Peleg is pleading for finally appears; read the 'crucifixion in his face' against 'Ahab has his humanities.'
Yojo's joke about fate disguised as chance, restated as the book's cosmology.
Ahab's own account of the 'sweet, resigned girl' Peleg mentions here.
Ishmael's cheerful acceptance of being paid and ordered about—the other side of the lay negotiation.
Where Ishmael first feared a cannibal; the word has now moved onto the ship.

ch17.essay:
I laughed out loud at this chapter and then felt caught. Ishmael opens with a genuinely generous paragraph—he respects everyone's religious obligations "never mind how comical," including ants worshipping a toad-stool and men bowing to a dead landlord's torso—and then spends the rest of the chapter unable to tolerate his friend sitting quietly on the floor for a day. The tolerance was easy in the abstract. The Ramadan, four feet from his bed, in the cold, drove him half mad.

The locked-door sequence is farce done with real craft: the chamber-maid's "La! la, ma'am!—Mistress! murder!", Mrs. Hussey with her mustard-pot and vinegar-cruet, the suicide sign she wants painted ("no suicides permitted here, and no smoking in the parlor"). Then the door bursts and there is Queequeg, "cool and self-collected," holding Yojo on his head like a man who has never once been in a hurry.

What I get out of the ending is how thoroughly Ishmael loses the argument. He delivers a lecture on hygiene and dyspepsia and the origins of hell in an undigested apple-dumpling—a lecture I half agree with—and Queequeg understands a third of it, is unmoved, and looks at him with "condescending concern and compassion." Melville lets the pagan have the last word, silently. And the throwaway about the feast where fifty enemies were cooked by evening is dropped in and abandoned with "No more, Queequeg." The book keeps refusing to make Queequeg safe.

annotations.quote: for we are all somehow dreadfully cracked about the head, and sadly need mending.
annotations.note: The book's most honest creed, and it comes from a man who is about to prove it by panicking over a locked door. Ishmael's theology: universal damage, universal mercy.

annotations.quote: hell is an idea first born on an undigested apple-dumpling
annotations.note: Ishmael's whole philosophy of religion reduced to indigestion. It's a joke, but it's also a serious materialist claim about where the doctrine of eternal punishment comes from—and he offers it to a man who has eaten people, without irony.

annotations.quote: He looked at me with a sort of condescending concern and compassion, as though he thought it a great pity that such a sensible young man should be so hopelessly lost to evangelical pagan piety.
annotations.note: The missionary position reversed. Every sentence Ishmael spoke could be turned around, and Queequeg turns it around without saying a word. Melville seems to relish giving the 'savage' the superior calm.

annotations.quote: so that the landlady should not make much profit by reason of his Ramadan
annotations.note: Queequeg fasts all day and then eats a breakfast large enough to erase the innkeeper's savings. A tiny act of economic justice, and a reminder that he is shrewd, not merely picturesque.

links.why: Ishmael's tolerant theology of 'the will of God' stated the first time, in warmer terms.
Queequeg's other great act of private ritual: building his own coffin and deciding not to die.

ch18.essay:
A short chapter with one great speech and one great throw. Bildad wants Queequeg's papers—proof he's converted—and Ishmael improvises the "First Congregational Church" of "this whole worshipping world," to which everyone belongs and in which the differences are only "queer crotchets." Peleg calls it a sermon. It is one, and it's better than Father Mapple's in a way: it demands nothing of anyone but that they admit they're all in the same boat, which they are about to be, literally.

Then Queequeg answers with his harpoon instead of his mouth. The tar spot on the water, the iron sailing over Bildad's hat, "spos-ee him whale-e eye; why, dad whale dead." Bildad's theological objections evaporate at once; he'll take a pagan who can throw. The ninetieth lay follows. The book keeps showing that the market has no religion; competence is the only creed that actually gets enforced.

And the signature. "Quohog. his X mark." Peleg can't hold Queequeg's name, and Queequeg copies a tattoo from his own arm—a figure whose meaning, we will learn much later, even he doesn't know. His identity on the ship's articles is a wrong name and an unreadable sign. I find that quietly devastating. The last image is Bildad, having preached the fiery pit, stooping to save a scrap of tarred twine. That is the man entire.

annotations.quote: the great and everlasting First Congregation of this whole worshipping world; we all belong to that; only some of us cherish some queer crotchets no ways touching the grand belief
annotations.note: Ishmael's improvised universalism. He means it as a dodge to get Queequeg aboard, but it's also the most generous religious statement in the book, and Peleg's 'splice hands' makes it a sailor's covenant.

annotations.quote: “Now,” said Queequeg, quietly hauling in the line, “spos-ee him whale-e eye; why, dad whale dead.”
annotations.note: Queequeg's rebuttal to the demand for conversion papers. The market doesn't care about his soul once it sees his arm. Note 'quietly'—he never performs; he just does the thing.

annotations.quote: Quohog. his X mark.
annotations.note: A wrong name and a tattoo he copies from his own arm. This is how Queequeg exists in the ship's records: misnamed, marked with a sign nobody—including him—can read. Keep it in mind for the coffin chapter.

annotations.quote: Pious harpooneers never make good voyagers—it takes the shark out of ’em
annotations.note: Peleg's counter-theology. Fear of hell makes you flinch from whales. He's arguing that salvation is bad for business, and the whole chapter agrees with him.

annotations.quote: Now and then he stooped to pick up a patch, or save an end of tarred twine, which otherwise might have been wasted.
annotations.note: After all the fiery-pit preaching, this is Bildad's real religion: nothing wasted. Melville ends the chapter on it without comment, and it's the truest portrait of him in the book.

links.why: The lay negotiation Queequeg is now subjected to; note how his skill changes Bildad's arithmetic.
Bildad's tract-pushing against Father Mapple's sermon—two Nantucket Christianities.

ch19.essay:
Elijah is the book's first outright prophet and Ishmael treats him exactly as I would: as a nuisance who might be a lunatic. What unsettles me on rereading is how much Elijah actually tells us—the three days Ahab lay like dead off Cape Horn, the fight before an altar in Santa, the silver calabash he spat into, the leg lost "according to the prophecy"—and how the book never explains any of it. These are fragments of a backstory that Melville deliberately leaves as fragments. The reader, like Ishmael, has to decide whether they're data or noise.

The "souls" exchange is my favorite bit. "Anything down there about your souls?"—as if the ship's articles might have a clause. Then: "A soul's a sort of a fifth wheel to a wagon." He's mocking, but he's also saying something true about what a whaleship asks of you. And then the pivot: He has enough soul "to make up for all deficiencies of that sort in other chaps." Ahab is not soulless; he's over-souled, and that's the danger.

Ishmael's final verdict—"a humbug"—arrives twice, and each time he has to work for it. He crosses the street to test whether Elijah is following. He is proud of his skepticism, and the book lets him keep it, because the alternative is to walk away from the ship, and nobody in this book ever walks away.

The prophet is named for the one who denounced [[ch16:Ahab of old|the biblical Ahab]], as Peleg has already half-admitted; the book plants its allusions and then has a character warn you not to mention them.

annotations.quote: A soul’s a sort of a fifth wheel to a wagon.
annotations.note: Delivered as a joke about sailors, it's really a description of the Pequod's economy: souls are surplus equipment. The ship will test whether that's true.

annotations.quote: _He’s_ got enough, though, to make up for all deficiencies of that sort in other chaps
annotations.note: Ahab's problem is not too little soul but too much. Elijah says it first and says it best; every later description of Ahab is a footnote to this.

annotations.quote: what’s signed, is signed; and what’s to be, will be; and then again, perhaps it won’t be, after all.
annotations.note: The prophet hedges his own prophecy. That 'perhaps it won't be' is what keeps Elijah from being a mere plot device: even he doesn't know if fate is fixed, and the book won't decide either.

annotations.quote: It is the easiest thing in the world for a man to look as if he had a great secret in him.
annotations.note: Ishmael's skepticism, and it's a good sentence. But the book is full of men who look as if they have a great secret in them—Ahab most of all—and every one of them turns out to actually have one.

annotations.quote: I pronounced him in my heart, a humbug.
annotations.note: He has to pronounce it twice, and cross a street to prove it. The insistence is the tell. Ishmael needs Elijah to be a humbug because otherwise he'd have to not sail.

links.why: The man Elijah is warning about, finally seen.
Peleg's version of the same warnings, framed as reassurance.
Elijah's second, stranger appearance at dawn.

ch20.essay:
A chapter about provisioning, and I think it's secretly about denial. The list is wonderful—pickles, quills, flannel for someone's rheumatic back, Aunt Charity bustling with an oil-ladle in one hand and a whaling lance in the other—and the joke about "spare everythings, almost, but a spare Captain and duplicate ship" is one of those Melville lines that only turns dark later, when you realize the lack of a spare captain is the plot.

But the paragraph that matters is the one where Ishmael admits he didn't want to look at his own doubt. He's signed on for three years under a man he has never seen, and "when a man suspects any wrong, it sometimes happens that if he be already involved in the matter, he insensibly strives to cover up his suspicions even from himself." That is as clear-eyed a sentence about sunk cost as I know. He said nothing "and tried to think nothing." Every crewman on the ship is doing the same thing, and the chapter shows you the mechanism before the voyage even starts.

Aunt Charity deserves her sentence. She is the only woman in the book who does anything, and what she does is make sure nothing is wanting—she owns "a score or two of well-saved dollars" in the ship, which means even her kindness is partly investment. Melville can't help noting it, and I like him for not pretending otherwise.

annotations.quote: Hence, the spare boats, spare spars, and spare lines and harpoons, and spare everythings, almost, but a spare Captain and duplicate ship.
annotations.note: A logistics joke that becomes the plot. The ship carries redundancy for everything except the one part that will fail.

annotations.quote: with a long oil-ladle in one hand, and a still longer whaling lance in the other
annotations.note: Aunt Charity, Quakeress, carrying the tools of both cooking and killing. Melville keeps putting domesticity and slaughter in the same hands; this is the book's honest picture of what the industry is.

annotations.quote: when a man suspects any wrong, it sometimes happens that if he be already involved in the matter, he insensibly strives to cover up his suspicions even from himself.
annotations.note: The psychology of the whole crew, stated before they sail. Ishmael can name it and still not act on it—which is what makes the naming honest rather than wise.

annotations.quote: I said nothing, and tried to think nothing.
annotations.note: Six words, and they're the hinge of the chapter. Not thinking is a choice here, and it's the one that ships him.

links.why: The sailing itself, two chapters on.
A whaling wife's side of the three-year absence, in the Rachel's captain.

ch21.essay:
The strangest chapter in the Nantucket section, and the one I understood least on first reading. Elijah's questions—did you see men going toward the ship? can you find them now?—are about the shadowy figures who'll turn out to be Fedallah's crew, and Ishmael half-sees them "too dim to be sure," then talks himself out of it. Melville is doing something bold: he gives you a supernatural hint and lets the narrator suppress it in real time. "I beat the thing down."

Then the tone swings completely. Queequeg sits on a sleeping rigger's rear end because "my country way," and explains that in his land the lower orders are fattened for use as ottomans, "much better than those garden-chairs which are convertible into walking-sticks." He flourishes his tomahawk over the man's head: "Perry easy, kill-e." I don't know how to feel about this and I think that's the intended condition. Ishmael's "it's grinding the face of the poor" is Isaiah, and it's a joke, and it's also an accurate description of the labor system the ship runs on.

And the last line: Ahab "remained invisibly enshrined within his cabin." Enshrined. The crew comes aboard in twos and threes and the captain is a relic in a reliquary. Twenty-one chapters in, we still haven't seen him. The withholding is beginning to feel like a pressure, which is exactly what it's for.

annotations.quote: Shan’t see ye again very soon, I guess; unless it’s before the Grand Jury.
annotations.note: Elijah's last words, and they assume a trial—someone will have to answer for what happens. The Epilogue is that testimony. He knows Ishmael is the witness before Ishmael does.

annotations.quote: But I beat the thing down
annotations.note: Ishmael suppressing a perception in real time. The dim figures were real. This is the book's method with the supernatural: shown, doubted, ignored, and later vindicated.

annotations.quote: it’s grinding the face of the poor.
annotations.note: Isaiah 3:15, applied to Queequeg sitting on a sleeping rigger. A joke, a Biblical allusion, and a literal description of how the ship's economy works, all in one line.

annotations.quote: the king, chiefs, and great people generally, were in the custom of fattening some of the lower orders for ottomans
annotations.note: Queequeg's furniture anecdote is grotesque and cheerful and I can't tell how seriously Melville wants it taken. What I notice is that Ishmael doesn't recoil—he just tells Queequeg to get off because the man is heavy.

annotations.quote: Meanwhile Captain Ahab remained invisibly enshrined within his cabin.
annotations.note: 'Enshrined'—the word for a saint's relics. The crew is being assembled around an unseen holy object. The book has spent twenty-one chapters not showing him, and this word explains why.

links.why: Elijah's first appearance.
The shadows Elijah asks about—Fedallah's crew—finally emerge.

ch22.essay:
Sailing on Christmas Day, and Melville makes almost nothing of the holiday except the title and one phrase—"a short, cold Christmas." The chapter is instead about the two old owners who cannot let go. Peleg kicks Ishmael in the rear (his "first kick") while Bildad sings psalms at the windlass over a crew roaring about the girls in Booble Alley. It's the sacred and profane heaving on the same rope, and the anchor comes up anyway.

What surprised me is how tender it becomes. Bildad, the skinflint who offered the 777th lay, lingers on deck, "looked everywhere and nowhere," and grips Peleg's hand by lantern-light. Peleg, the blusterer, has a tear "when the lantern came too near." And then Bildad's farewell speech, which is one of the funniest and saddest things in the book: prayers and cheese in the same breath, "beware of fornication" and "be careful with the butter—twenty cents the pound it was." He cannot separate his love for the ship from his ledger, and I don't think Melville wants him to. That is what love looks like in a man like that.

The hymn matters. "Sweet fields beyond the swelling flood" is Watts on the Jordan and Canaan, and Ishmael hears it as pure hope—"many a pleasant haven in store." He's wrong, and the book knows it, and the final sentence corrects him: three "heavy-hearted cheers," and "blindly plunged like fate into the lone Atlantic." Blindly. Like fate. The voyage begins with the ship's own eyes shut.

What I keep coming back to is that Bildad weeps. The man who tried to cheat Ishmael in [[ch16|The Ship]] cannot leave the rail. Melville gives the miser the last human moment before the sea, and I think it is deliberate: the shore's pieties are not fake, they are just useless where the ship is going.

annotations.quote: Nevertheless, not three days previous, Bildad had told them that no profane songs would be allowed on board the Pequod
annotations.note: The rule lasts exactly until the anchor needs raising. Bildad sings psalms; the men sing Booble Alley; the work gets done. The book's picture of how religion and labor actually coexist.

annotations.quote: That was my first kick.
annotations.note: Four words, and a whole history of hierarchy at sea. Ishmael counts it like a rite of passage. The merchant service, we were told, would be damned; this is the whaling service's welcome.

annotations.quote: whose freezing spray cased us in ice, as in polished armor
annotations.note: The first image of the ship at sea, and she's already armored—for a fight, not a fishing trip. Melville's similes keep telling you what kind of book this is before the plot does.

annotations.quote: Never did those sweet words sound more sweetly to me than then. They were full of hope and fruition.
annotations.note: Ishmael hearing Watts's hymn about Canaan as a promise. The reader who knows the ending hears it as a hymn about crossing the river of death—which is what it actually is.

annotations.quote: looked everywhere and nowhere; and at last, mechanically coiling a rope upon its pin
annotations.note: Bildad unable to leave. The 'mechanically coiling a rope' is the tell: a man whose feelings have nowhere to go except into his hands. Melville is so good at old men.

annotations.quote: Be careful with the butter—twenty cents the pound it was, and mind ye, if—”
annotations.note: Cut off mid-sentence, still doing accounts. It would be cruel satire if the previous paragraph hadn't shown him weeping. Instead it's the most loving thing he knows how to say.

annotations.quote: we gave three heavy-hearted cheers, and blindly plunged like fate into the lone Atlantic.
annotations.note: 'Blindly' and 'like fate' in the same clause. The ship sets out sightless, and the narrator who will survive to tell it already knows. This sentence is the whole novel's trajectory compressed.

links.why: The night this chapter ends on, and the man at the helm.
Bildad at the lay negotiation, for contrast with Bildad weeping at the rail.
Ahab's own account of forty years of such departures.

ch23.essay:
Six paragraphs, and Melville calls it a "six-inch chapter" and "the stoneless grave of Bulkington." I think it is the most concentrated piece of philosophy in the book, and I want to be explicit about why, because on a first read it can go by as a purple flourish about a minor sailor. Bulkington was glimpsed once, at the Spouter-Inn ([[ch3:noble shoulders|the man with the 'noble shoulders' whom the crew followed out into the dark]]), just back from four years at sea. Now he is at the helm on the Pequod's first night out, unable to stay on land: "The land seemed scorching to his feet." Most scholars think Melville meant him for a larger role and abandoned the plan as the book changed under his hands; what remains is a character-sized hole with a hymn poured into it. Whether or not that is the history, the effect is the point. Bulkington is buried in the chapter that names him, and the burial is what lets the chapter say what it says.

The argument is built on a real piece of seamanship, and it helps to see the machine before the metaphor. A ship caught in a gale near a lee shore—wind blowing toward the land—cannot run for harbor, because the same wind that would carry her home would carry her onto the rocks; "one touch of land, though it but graze the keel, would make her shudder through and through." So she must do the thing that looks like madness: crowd on sail and fight *away* from safety, out into open water, "for refuge's sake forlornly rushing into peril." Every sailor reading in 1851 knew this was literally true. Melville's move is to treat it as also true of the mind. "All deep, earnest thinking is but the intrepid effort of the soul to keep the open independence of her sea." A conclusion is a coast. A comfort is a coast. The list of what the port offers—"safety, comfort, hearthstone, supper, warm blankets, friends, all that's kind to our mortalities"—is not sneered at; it is tender, and it has to be, or the rejection would cost nothing.

Then the sentence I have argued with for years: "as in landlessness alone resides highest truth, shoreless, indefinite as God—so, better is it to perish in that howling infinite, than be ingloriously dashed upon the lee, even if that were safety!" Notice what it equates. God with indefiniteness. Truth with having no ground under you. Death at sea with apotheosis. I do not think this is simply Melville's creed; it is the creed of a man who cannot stay home, dressed as a universal law, and the chapter half-knows it. That is why it is an apostrophe, a shout at Bulkington, rather than an argument. But the reason it is not merely a mood is that the whole book obeys it as a method. Every cetology chapter, every digression on ropes or paintings or the whale's tail, is Ishmael crowding sail off shore, refusing to let the book land on a meaning. When Ishmael says in [[ch32:draught of a draught|Cetology]] that the whole book is "but a draught of a draught," that is the Lee Shore applied to composition.

There is a darker reading, which I also hold. The "howling infinite" is where Ahab is going, and he is going there on purpose. If landlessness is highest truth, then Ahab's refusal of every port—the Rachel's captain begging him to [[ch128:my boy|help search for a lost son]], Starbuck's plea to turn for Nantucket in [[ch132]]—is not madness but consistency. The chapter that deifies Bulkington for perishing is quietly also the chapter that licenses Ahab. Melville keeps both possibilities open, which is why the closing line is a paradox and not a consolation: "Up from the spray of thy ocean-perishing—straight up, leaps thy apotheosis!" A man made a god by drowning. Watch for the pattern; it is how the book treats every one of its heroes, and in the [[ch135:sink all coffins|last chapter]] Ahab claims it for himself with his own mouth.

annotations.quote: The land seemed scorching to his feet.
annotations.note: Bulkington has been home a few days after four years at sea and cannot bear it. The image is of someone who literally cannot stand on solid ground. Melville is describing a temperament, and I think it is his own—he shipped out again within weeks of every homecoming in his twenties.

annotations.quote: Wonderfullest things are ever the unmentionable; deep memories yield no epitaphs; this six-inch chapter is the stoneless grave of Bulkington.
annotations.note: Melville buries a character in a chapter and tells you he is doing it. A man too large to write about gets the shortest chapter. I read it as the book's most honest admission that its biggest subjects cannot be said, only pointed at—the same admission that opens [[ch42:It was the whiteness of the whale that above|The Whiteness of the Whale]], where Ishmael says he must explain himself 'else all these chapters might be naught.'

annotations.quote: in the port is safety, comfort, hearthstone, supper, warm blankets, friends, all that’s kind to our mortalities.
annotations.note: He lists everything good in life, and then says the ship must fly from it. The list is not sneered at—'all that's kind to our mortalities' is tender. That tenderness is what makes the rejection cost something, and it is the same list Starbuck will lay before Ahab in [[ch132]] when he begs him to turn home.

annotations.quote: for refuge’s sake forlornly rushing into peril; her only friend her bitterest foe!
annotations.note: The seamanship is exact: on a lee shore the open sea that could drown you is the only thing that can save you. Melville loves these inversions where the safe thing kills and the dangerous thing preserves—the coffin that becomes a [[ch126|life-buoy]] is the same figure carved in wood.

annotations.quote: all deep, earnest thinking is but the intrepid effort of the soul to keep the open independence of her sea
annotations.note: Thinking as seamanship: not reaching a conclusion but keeping off the rocks of one. This is the line that justifies the book's whole digressive shape. Every cetology chapter is Ishmael crowding sail off shore, and the refusal to say what the whale means is not evasion but this creed practiced.

annotations.quote: But as in landlessness alone resides highest truth, shoreless, indefinite as God—so, better is it to perish in that howling infinite, than be ingloriously dashed upon the lee, even if that were safety!
annotations.note: A creed I keep arguing with. It equates God with indefiniteness and truth with having no ground under you. It is also, quietly, a prediction of how the book will end—perishing in the infinite rather than reaching port—and a license for Ahab, who refuses every harbor offered him. Whether you find it heroic or monstrous will probably decide how you read the last three chapters.

annotations.quote: Up from the spray of thy ocean-perishing—straight up, leaps thy apotheosis!
annotations.note: Bulkington is deified in advance of his death, which we never see. A pattern: Melville's heroes are made gods by drowning. Ahab claims the same apotheosis for himself, in almost the same words, in [[ch135:sink all coffins|the last chapter]].

links.why: Bulkington's only other appearance—one paragraph at the Spouter-Inn—so you can see how little the 'grave' contains.
The Lee Shore as a method of composition: the book that refuses to finish.
Starbuck offers Ahab the port—hearthstone, wife, child—and Ahab refuses it, as this chapter says he must.
Ahab's own apotheosis-by-drowning, the payoff of this chapter's last line.
The coffin turned life-buoy: the same inversion of peril and safety, in wood.

ch24.essay:
Ishmael as lawyer, and I find him more persuasive than he has any right to be. The case for whaling's dignity is argued in a courtroom voice—"But this is not the half; look again"—and it mixes real facts (the Dunkirk Nantucketers, the British bounties, seven hundred ships and eighteen thousand men) with outrageous claims (the whale-ship liberated Peru; the whale-ship is "the true mother" of Australia). What I take from it is that he half-believes the outrageous parts, and that the mix is the point: whaling really did open the Pacific, and the industry really was, as he says, everywhere and honored nowhere.

The best sentence is the one about butchers. "Butchers we are, that is true. But butchers, also, and butchers of the bloodiest badge have been all Martial Commanders whom the world invariably delights to honor." That's a fair hit. And then the lamps: the whole world burns sperm oil "as before so many shrines, to our glory." Every candle is a tribute to a trade nobody will admit to admiring.

The chapter ends by turning personal in a way that makes me sit up. If there is any "undiscovered prime thing" in him, if his creditors find "precious MSS." in his desk, the credit goes to whaling, "for a whale-ship was my Yale College and my Harvard." Melville had been to sea and not to college; the sentence is his own. It's also a warning about the book you're holding: it's going to be a whale-ship, not a lecture hall.

annotations.quote: For what are the comprehensible terrors of man compared with the interlinked terrors and wonders of God!
annotations.note: The argument for whaling's dignity turns theological here: soldiers face what men do, whalemen face what God made. It's a boast, but it's also the book's real subject announced in a sentence.

annotations.quote: for almost all the tapers, lamps, and candles that burn round the globe, burn, as before so many shrines, to our glory!
annotations.note: The whole lit world as an altar to whaling. There's a bitterness under the pride: the trade is everywhere in daily life and honored nowhere. That's still true of most trades.

annotations.quote: Ah, the world! Oh, the world!
annotations.note: After a paragraph of listing what anonymous Nantucketers did that Cook gets credit for, Ishmael just sighs at it. The two exclamations are the sound of an argument giving up and becoming grief.

annotations.quote: Drive down your hat in presence of the Czar, and take it off to Queequeg!
annotations.note: The chapter's real politics. All the imperial and royal name-dropping has been leading here: the harpooneer outranks the emperor. Melville's democracy is sincere, and it's going to be argued more solemnly in two chapters.

annotations.quote: for a whale-ship was my Yale College and my Harvard.
annotations.note: Melville's own biography surfacing through Ishmael. Whatever this book turns out to be, he's telling you where its education came from—and asking you to weigh that against the universities.

links.why: Ishmael's other great defense of his subject—by classifying it.
The same argument for whaling's honor, made through myth.
Where he first explained why he goes to sea.

ch25.essay:
Three paragraphs of pure mischief, and I love that Melville kept it in. Having argued whaling's dignity with facts, the advocate now adds "a not unreasonable surmise": kings are anointed with oil at their coronations, and what oil could it possibly be but sperm oil? Therefore "we whalemen supply your kings and queens with coronation stuff!"

The route to that punchline goes through hair-oil. A grown man who uses it "has probably got a quoggy spot in him somewhere"—one of those Melville aside-verdicts that feels like a friend leaning over at a party. And the king's head is oiled "even as a head of salad," and perhaps "with a view of making its interior run well, as they anoint machinery." Monarchy reduced to lubrication in a paragraph.

I don't think this is filler. It's the book teaching you its manners: after every earnest passage there's a wink, and the wink is often where the real subversion lives. A sailor's oil on a sovereign's skull—the lowest trade touching the highest office. That's the same joke as "take it off to Queequeg," told sideways.

annotations.quote: Certain I am, however, that a king’s head is solemnly oiled at his coronation, even as a head of salad.
annotations.note: Monarchy as salad dressing. The comic register is doing serious democratic work: nothing about a king's head is different in kind from a lettuce.

annotations.quote: a mature man who uses hair-oil, unless medicinally, that man has probably got a quoggy spot in him somewhere.
annotations.note: An unprovoked verdict on hair-oil, delivered with the confidence of a maxim. I include it because it's the voice of the book at its most companionable—opinions about everything, delivered as if to a friend.

annotations.quote: Think of that, ye loyal Britons! we whalemen supply your kings and queens with coronation stuff!
annotations.note: The whole 'Advocate' argument ends on a shrug of a joke. That's the rhythm to learn: earnest, then absurd, and the absurd part often says the true thing more plainly.

links.why: The chapter this is a postscript to.
The other odd royal substance: ambergris.

ch26.essay:
The first "Knights and Squires" is really two chapters welded at a seam you can see: a portrait of Starbuck, exact and cool, and then a hymn that bursts out of the portrait as if Melville could not hold it in. I want to walk through both, because the hymn is the passage on which the whole book's claim to be a tragedy depends, and the portrait is where you are told, in advance, how the tragedy will go.

The Starbuck half works by a series of physical observations that are secretly moral ones. His thinness is "merely the condensation of the man"—no water lost to feeling. His courage "was not a sentiment; but a thing simply useful," and he thinks of it as a ship's store "like her beef and her bread, and not to be foolishly wasted." This is the practical man's ethics, and it explains everything Starbuck does later: why he will not lower after sundown, why he counts the cost of Ahab's chase in barrels of oil on the [[ch36|quarter-deck]], why he cannot draw on the whole store at once when the moment demands it. "I will have no man in my boat who is not afraid of a whale" is, I think, the sanest sentence anyone speaks in this book, and Melville immediately glosses it—an utterly fearless man is more dangerous than a coward—and then hands the ship to exactly such a man. Then a single sentence gives Starbuck a graveyard: his father, his brother, both taken by whales, "Where, in the bottomless deeps, could he find the torn limbs of his brother?" Melville grants this history in one line and never mentions it again. It is enough. You know now why caution is not cowardice in him.

And then the verdict, delivered before Ahab has spoken a word. Starbuck's bravery can stand up to "seas, or winds, or whales" but "cannot withstand those more terrific, because more spiritual terrors, which sometimes menace you from the concentrating brow of an enraged and mighty man." I find this the book's most painful piece of foreshadowing precisely because it is delivered with such respect. Starbuck is not weak; he is reasonable, and the chapter is telling you that reason has no traction against will. When you reach [[ch123:wrestling with an angel|The Musket]], where he stands outside Ahab's door with a loaded gun and cannot fire, remember that you were told here, and that Melville said he could scarcely bear to write it: "it is a thing most sorrowful, nay shocking, to expose the fall of valour in the soul."

That sentence is the hinge. The narrator, in the act of dreading what he must do to Starbuck, turns to the reader and asks, in advance, for a covering of "costliest robes" over the coming shame. And then the plea widens into the hymn. If he is going to give "meanest mariners, and renegades and castaways" tragic dignity, "weave round them tragic graces," "spread a rainbow over his disastrous set of sun"—then "bear me out in it, thou just Spirit of Equality." What is he asking permission for? For the book. In 1851 tragedy belonged to kings; the whole apparatus of high seriousness was reserved for people with robes. Melville is claiming it for a whaling crew, and he grounds the claim in a theology: God as "the centre and circumference of all democracy," whose "omnipresence" is "our divine equality." Then the examples—Bunyan the convict, Cervantes with his maimed arm, Andrew Jackson "from the pebbles"—all greatness "hurled" up from the bottom. Jackson dates the passage and does not damage it; the point is the shape.

I am never sure whether to be moved or embarrassed by the hymn, and I have settled on moved, for a reason I can state. Everything the book does with Ahab depends on this paragraph being true. If a one-legged Nantucket whaling captain cannot carry tragic weight, then [[ch36|the quarter-deck speech]] is a rant, [[ch132|The Symphony]] is sentiment, and the [[ch135|three days' chase]] is an accident at sea. Melville knew this, and rather than assume it he stopped the novel to ask for it. The asking is the humility that makes the rest of the book's arrogance possible.

annotations.quote: It was merely the condensation of the man.
annotations.note: Starbuck described as reduced to essentials, no water lost to feeling. Melville's physical descriptions are always moral: this is what a reasonable man looks like when there is no excess to spare. Compare the description of Ahab in [[ch28]], which is all fire and bronze—the two men are drawn in opposite materials on purpose.

annotations.quote: “I will have no man in my boat,” said Starbuck, “who is not afraid of a whale.”
annotations.note: The most sensible line in the book, and Melville immediately glosses it: an utterly fearless man is more dangerous than a coward. The book is about to be commanded by exactly that man. Starbuck will say a version of this to Ahab's face in [[ch36|The Quarter-Deck]] and be answered with a speech about pasteboard masks.

annotations.quote: courage was one of the great staple outfits of the ship, like her beef and her bread, and not to be foolishly wasted
annotations.note: Courage as provision, with a finite supply. It is the practical man's ethics, and it explains why Starbuck will not lower after sundown—and why he will be helpless when someone demands the whole store at once. Ahab's courage, by contrast, is not a store but a fire, and fires do not ration.

annotations.quote: What doom was his own father’s? Where, in the bottomless deeps, could he find the torn limbs of his brother?
annotations.note: Two questions, no answers. Starbuck's caution has a graveyard under it: father and brother both taken by whales. Melville grants him this history in one line and never mentions it again, and it is enough to make his later timidity read as grief rather than weakness.

annotations.quote: yet cannot withstand those more terrific, because more spiritual terrors, which sometimes menace you from the concentrating brow of an enraged and mighty man.
annotations.note: The verdict on Starbuck, delivered before Ahab has spoken a word. His failure is announced with something like tenderness: reason is brave against nature and helpless against will. The scene this predicts is [[ch123:wrestling with an angel|The Musket]], where he stands at Ahab's door with a loaded gun.

annotations.quote: for it is a thing most sorrowful, nay shocking, to expose the fall of valour in the soul.
annotations.note: The narrator confesses in advance that he can hardly bear what he is going to do to this character. I know of few novels where the author flinches on the page like this, and it is the flinch that turns the portrait into the hymn that follows.

annotations.quote: man, in the ideal, is so noble and so sparkling, such a grand and glowing creature, that over any ignominious blemish in him all his fellows should run to throw their costliest robes.
annotations.note: Melville's humanism stated as a plea. He is asking the reader in advance to cover Starbuck's coming shame. I find it disarming that he cares this much for a character's dignity—and note that the robes are a king's robes, which the next paragraph will give to a whaleman.

annotations.quote: that democratic dignity which, on all hands, radiates without end from God; Himself! The great God absolute! The centre and circumference of all democracy!
annotations.note: God as the source of equality, not of hierarchy. This is 1851 American theology at its boldest, and it is the license Melville claims for making a tragedy out of a whaleman. Without this sentence, Ahab is a case study; with it he is Lear.

annotations.quote: If, then, to meanest mariners, and renegades and castaways, I shall hereafter ascribe high qualities, though dark; weave round them tragic graces
annotations.note: This is the book's contract with the reader, stated plainly: sailors will be treated as tragic heroes. 'Castaways' is not idle—[[ch93|The Castaway]] is the title of Pip's chapter, and Pip is the most abased of them all, the one who is 'lifted to the exalted mounts' by going mad.

annotations.quote: Thou who didst pick up Andrew Jackson from the pebbles; who didst hurl him upon a war-horse; who didst thunder him higher than a throne!
annotations.note: Jackson, of all people, as proof of democratic election by God. It dates the passage and does not matter; the point is the shape—greatness hurled up from the bottom—which is also the shape of the book's own ambition and of Ahab's, the 'poor old whale-hunter' who takes on the sun.

links.why: The scene this chapter predicts: Starbuck with the musket, unable to act.
Starbuck's reason meets Ahab's will for the first time, and loses.
Ahab's portrait, drawn in fire and bronze to Starbuck's biscuit and iron.
'Castaways' given tragic grace—Pip, the least of the crew, made a seer.
The second Knights and Squires: Stubb, Flask, and the harpooneers, the men this hymn is also for.

ch27.essay:
Stubb and Flask and the three harpooneers, and then a paragraph that quietly becomes one of the book's most important. Stubb first: "Long usage had, for this Stubb, converted the jaws of death into an easy chair." He smokes constantly, and Ishmael suggests the tobacco works "as a sort of disinfecting agent" against the "nameless miseries of the numberless mortals who have died exhaling" the air. I've never been able to read that without thinking it's true of most cheerfulness—a filter against the atmosphere. Flask is simpler: he thinks the whale is "a species of magnified mouse," a man with no reverence and therefore no fear.

Tashtego and Daggoo are drawn with a mix of genuine admiration and the racial vocabulary of 1851, and I don't want to pretend that's not there. What I notice is the direction of the comparisons: a white man before Daggoo is "a white flag come to beg truce of a fortress," and Flask, his officer, "looked like a chess-man beside him." The hierarchy of the ship and the hierarchy of the men point opposite ways, and Melville says so: Americans provide "the brains, the rest of the world as generously supplying the muscles." That's an observation, not an endorsement, and it's still accurate about a lot of industries.

Then the word: Isolatoes. "Not acknowledging the common continent of men, but each Isolato living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, federated along one keel." An "Anacharsis Clootz deputation"—the delegation of all humanity that showed up at the French Revolution—sailing to "lay the world's grievances before that bar from which not very many of them ever come back." And then, out of nowhere, Pip. "He never did—oh, no! he went before." The book tells you, in a chapter about crew rosters, who is going to die first and how he'll be received in heaven.

annotations.quote: Long usage had, for this Stubb, converted the jaws of death into an easy chair.
annotations.note: Stubb's whole character. Not brave, not cowardly—habituated. Melville seems to suspect that most people survive terror this way, and to half admire it and half find it appalling.

annotations.quote: Stubb’s tobacco smoke might have operated as a sort of disinfecting agent.
annotations.note: Cheerfulness as a filter against the exhaled misery of everyone who ever died. It's a joke about pipes, and it's one of the book's saddest theories of temperament.

annotations.quote: the wondrous whale was but a species of magnified mouse, or at least water-rat
annotations.note: Flask's error is the absence of wonder. The book will argue that seeing the whale as a mouse is a failure of perception, not of courage—and that it's Flask, not Ahab, who's simply wrong about what a whale is.

annotations.quote: a white man standing before him seemed a white flag come to beg truce of a fortress.
annotations.note: Melville reverses the ship's hierarchy in a simile. Daggoo is the third mate's subordinate and the third mate is a chess-piece beside him. The book keeps noting that rank and stature don't line up.

annotations.quote: the native American liberally provides the brains, the rest of the world as generously supplying the muscles.
annotations.note: A plain description of how American labor was organized in 1851, in whaling and canals and railroads alike. The irony in 'liberally' and 'generously' is Ishmael's; the arrangement is real.

annotations.quote: _Isolatoes_ too, I call such, not acknowledging the common continent of men, but each _Isolato_ living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, federated along one keel
annotations.note: Melville coins a word for the crew and it's the book's social theory: islands, temporarily a nation. 'Federated along one keel' is America, and it's also every group of strangers who've ever had to work together.

annotations.quote: Black Little Pip—he never did—oh, no! he went before. Poor Alabama boy!
annotations.note: Pip's fate announced in an aside, in a chapter about the crew list, hundreds of pages early. 'Called a coward here, hailed a hero there'—the book's judgment on him is delivered before we meet him. Nothing in Moby-Dick is a surprise; everything is a fulfillment.

links.why: Starbuck's portrait, and the hymn that licenses this one.
The crew as a chorus, in their own voices.
Stubb's 'laughing' philosophy tested on a cook and a whale steak.

ch28.essay:
Twenty-eight chapters, and here he is. I think the delay is the most important structural decision in the book, and it is worth being precise about what it accomplishes. By now Ahab is made entirely of other people's sentences: Peleg's "[[ch16:ungodly, god-like|grand, ungodly, god-like man]]," the Bildad paragraph's "[[ch16:all mortal greatness is but disease|all mortal greatness is but disease]]," Elijah's [[ch19|hints on the wharf]] about something that happened off Cape Horn, the word "enshrined." Ishmael has been checking the taffrail every time he comes on deck. So when the man appears, he has to be seen through a dozen rumors, and Melville makes the first sight nothing but presence: "Reality outran apprehension; Captain Ahab stood upon his quarter-deck." No description for another sentence. The pressure of twenty-seven chapters breaks on six words, and the words say only that he is *there*.

Then the description, and I want to point out its method, because it is how Melville will handle Ahab for the rest of the book. Every physical detail is a metaphor and every metaphor is physical. He looks "like a man cut away from the stake, when the fire has overrunningly wasted all the limbs without consuming them"—a man burned and not destroyed. His form is "solid bronze," cast "like Cellini's Perseus." The scar is a lightning-seam down the trunk of a great tree, "leaving the tree still greenly alive, but branded." Notice what these three images share: in each, something elemental has gone through him and he has survived it, changed. Ahab is never described as a man who has a wound; he is described as what is left after a force has passed. And the crew argue about whether the scar was born with him or struck into him—the Gay Head Indian says it came at forty in "an elemental strife at sea," the Manxman says a birth-mark "from crown to sole." The book never settles this, and that is the question about Ahab: whether his nature was struck into him by the whale or was always there, waiting for a whale to name it. The later chapter [[ch41:his intellect|Moby Dick]] will tell you how the monomania hired his intellect; this chapter tells you the intellect was always in a body shaped like this.

Then the posture, which is the chapter's masterpiece of carpentry. An auger hole, half an inch, bored into the deck on each side of the quarter-deck. "His bone leg steadied in that hole; one arm elevated, and holding by a shroud; Captain Ahab stood erect." He is physically pegged to his ship. A man who cannot move and will not be moved, "looking straight out beyond the ship's ever-pitching prow," with "unsurrenderable wilfulness" in the glance. First-time readers sometimes take the ivory leg as a mere emblem of the wound; look instead at the hole. The ship has been drilled to receive him, and he stands in it the way the mast stands in its step. When the leg later [[ch106|splinters]] and the [[ch108|carpenter]] makes him another, the question of what Ahab stands on gets asked again literally.

The phrase that stops me is "a crucifixion in his face." Ishmael does not say Ahab looks like Christ; he says the suffering is on his face the way it is on a crucifix—"the nameless regal overbearing dignity of some mighty woe." Peleg said Ahab has his humanities. This paragraph says the humanities are what is being crucified, and it is careful to leave the cross unnamed. You will not be told what Ahab is nailed to until he tells you himself, on the [[ch36:pasteboard masks|quarter-deck]], and even then it will be in the form of a theory rather than a confession.

And then the ending, which is the sentence I find saddest in the chapter. The weather warms; the "red-cheeked, dancing girls, April and May" come home to the winter woods; even the thunder-cloven oak sends out a few sprouts. "More than once did he put forth the faint blossom of a look, which, in any other man, would have soon flowered out in a smile." In any other man. Melville lets you feel how close Ahab is to ordinary warmth and then closes the door, gently, with a conditional. It is the same move [[ch132|The Symphony]] will make at full length, a hundred chapters on, when Ahab drops a tear into the sea and Starbuck thinks for a moment he has him. He does not. The blossom never flowers here either, and the chapter ends on the not-quite, which is where Ahab lives.

annotations.quote: Reality outran apprehension; Captain Ahab stood upon his quarter-deck.
annotations.note: After twenty-eight chapters of rumor, six words of fact. No description yet—just that he is there. The delay has turned Ahab into a pressure, and this sentence is the pressure breaking. Everything you know about him so far came from [[ch16|Peleg]] and [[ch19|Elijah]]; this is the first thing Ishmael sees for himself.

annotations.quote: He looked like a man cut away from the stake, when the fire has overrunningly wasted all the limbs without consuming them
annotations.note: Ahab's first description is of a man who has been burned and not destroyed. Everything after—the bronze, the lightning-scar—keeps this note: he is what is left after something elemental went through him. Fire will be his element to the end; in [[ch119:speechless, placeless power|The Candles]] he tells the lightning that he was once burned by it and bears the scar.

annotations.quote: leaving the tree still greenly alive, but branded.
annotations.note: The scar as lightning down a tree trunk. What I notice is 'greenly alive'—the image insists that the strike did not kill him, which is somehow worse than if it had. He is a living thing marked by a force, and the book will keep asking whether the force was outside him or was him.

annotations.quote: then, whoever should do that last office for the dead, would find a birth-mark on him from crown to sole.
annotations.note: The Manxman's rumor: the scar goes all the way down; it is not a wound but a nature. The book never resolves whether Ahab was struck or born this way, and that is the central question about him. Note who is speaking—the same old Manxman who will read omens in [[ch125|the log-line]] and hear the drowned in the seals' cries.

annotations.quote: “Aye, he was dismasted off Japan,” said the old Gay-Head Indian once; “but like his dismasted craft, he shipped another mast without coming home for it. He has a quiver of ’em.”
annotations.note: The crew's idiom makes Ahab's body a ship: the leg is a mast, and he carries spares. It is a joke, and it is also how the book thinks. Ahab and the Pequod are one thing; when the leg breaks in [[ch106]] the carpenter is called as if to repair a spar.

annotations.quote: His bone leg steadied in that hole; one arm elevated, and holding by a shroud; Captain Ahab stood erect
annotations.note: An auger hole bored into the deck for his ivory leg. He is physically pegged to the ship, stepped into it like a mast. The image of a man who cannot move and will not be moved, in one detail of carpentry—and a first-time reader will do well to picture it exactly, because Ahab will stand in this hole for most of the book.

annotations.quote: moody stricken Ahab stood before them with a crucifixion in his face
annotations.note: Not 'like Christ'—'a crucifixion in his face.' The suffering is the point, not the sanctity. Melville is careful: this is a man being tortured on something, and we do not yet know what. He will name it himself on the [[ch36:pasteboard masks|quarter-deck]], as a theory of masks.

annotations.quote: as ever all clouds choose the loftiest peaks to pile themselves upon.
annotations.note: Ahab's gloom as weather on a mountain. The simile makes his suffering a function of his height, and the book will keep insisting that his misery and his greatness are the same fact—the claim first made, before we met him, in [[ch16:all mortal greatness is but disease|the Bildad paragraph]].

annotations.quote: More than once did he put forth the faint blossom of a look, which, in any other man, would have soon flowered out in a smile.
annotations.note: 'In any other man.' Melville shows you how near Ahab is to ordinary warmth and then closes the door with a conditional. Rereading, this is the sentence I find saddest in the chapter, and it is the seed of [[ch132|The Symphony]], where the same near-thaw happens at full length and fails the same way.

links.why: Everything Ishmael 'knew' about Ahab before this moment came from Peleg.
Ahab finally speaks, and names what the crucifixion is on.
Ishmael's account of how the wound became a monomania—the history behind this portrait.
The 'faint blossom of a look' given a whole chapter, and the same ending.
Ahab and fire: the burned man addresses the lightning.

ch29.essay:
The title is a stage direction, and it announces what the book is about to become: a play. From here Ahab will get soliloquies, entrances, and exits, and the prose will slip into blank verse whenever he opens his mouth. The chapter's opening is almost drunk on weather—days like "crystal goblets of Persian sherbet," nights like "haughty dames in jewelled velvets"—and then the sentence that turns it: all this beauty "inward turned upon the soul," and "more and more they wrought on Ahab's texture." Pleasant weather makes him worse. That tells you everything about the direction he's pointed.

Then Ahab and Stubb. Stubb, who converted death into an easy chair, makes one tentative suggestion—muffle the ivory heel with tow so the men can sleep—and Ahab calls him a dog and threatens to "clear the world of thee." It's the first time we hear Ahab speak, and what he says is: "Below to thy nightly grave; where such as ye sleep between shrouds, to use ye to the filling one at last." He can't mention a bed without a coffin. Even the cabin scuttle is "going down into one's tomb."

Stubb's monologue afterward is my favorite thing in the chapter, because it's an ordinary man trying to think and finding he can't. Strike him or pray for him? "Think not, is my eleventh commandment; and sleep when you can, is my twelfth." And the detail about Ahab's pillow "a sort of frightful hot, as though a baked brick had been on it," from the steward—the crew are already collecting evidence about their captain, the way you'd watch a fire you can't put out. "Damn me, but all things are queer, come to think of 'em. But that's against my principles." That's most of us, and Stubb knows it, and goes back to bed.

Read it with [[ch31|Queen Mab]] open: Stubb's dream is this scene digested overnight, and the fact that he decides the kick was an honor tells you how the crew will metabolize Ahab from here on.

annotations.quote: Inward they turned upon the soul, especially when the still mild hours of eve came on
annotations.note: Beautiful weather makes Ahab worse. Everything the world offers as consolation turns inward on him and becomes fuel. This is the first clear sign that his condition isn't something the voyage can cure.

annotations.quote: “It feels like going down into one’s tomb,”—he would mutter to himself—“for an old captain like me to be descending this narrow scuttle, to go to my grave-dug berth.”
annotations.note: Ahab's first quoted words in the book, and they're about his own burial. He can't go to bed without rehearsing death. The tomb-scuttle image will return at the very end.

annotations.quote: Some considering touch of humanity was in him
annotations.note: He muffles his own step so the mates can sleep. Melville keeps giving you these grains of Ahab's decency, and they're never enough to change anything—which is the tragedy's exact shape.

annotations.quote: Below to thy nightly grave; where such as ye sleep between shrouds, to use ye to the filling one at last.—Down, dog, and kennel!
annotations.note: Stubb asks for quiet and gets told that his hammock is practice for his coffin. 'Shrouds' means both rigging and burial cloth. Ahab's first speech is a pun on death, delivered as an insult.

annotations.quote: somehow, now, I don’t well know whether to go back and strike him, or—what’s that?—down here on my knees and pray for him?
annotations.note: Stubb's confusion is the crew's whole relationship to Ahab: rage and reverence with nothing in between. That he's never prayed before and thinks of it now is the chapter's real event.

annotations.quote: and the pillow a sort of frightful hot, as though a baked brick had been on it
annotations.note: Evidence gathered by a steward. The crew are already investigating Ahab like a fever. This detail is more frightening than any speech because it's so domestic.

annotations.quote: Think not, is my eleventh commandment; and sleep when you can, is my twelfth
annotations.note: Stubb's creed, and it's the opposite of Bulkington's in 'The Lee Shore.' One man keeps the open sea of thought; the other refuses to think on principle. The book respects both and follows neither.

annotations.quote: Damn me, but all things are queer, come to think of ’em. But that’s against my principles.
annotations.note: Stubb touches the edge of the book's vertigo—everything is strange if you look—and backs away. I find this line very funny and a little heartbreaking. He's right, and he can't afford to be.

links.why: The still portrait this chapter sets in motion.
Stubb's dream about the kick—what this scene does to him overnight.
The pipe Ahab throws away, immediately after.

ch30.essay:
One page. Ahab lights his pipe at the binnacle lamp, sits on his ivory stool—"a Khan of the plank, and a king of the sea"—and finds that smoking no longer soothes. The throne of narwhale tusks is the book at its most kingly; the pipe going into the sea is the book at its most exact. Everything gentle in him is being discarded, one object at a time. Last chapter it was sleep. This chapter it's tobacco.

What I love is the reasoning. He's been "ignorantly smoking to windward all the while"—the smoke blowing back into his own face—"with such nervous whiffs, as if, like the dying whale, my final jets were the strongest and fullest of trouble." He compares himself to the animal he's hunting, at the moment of its death, without seeming to notice. The pipe is "meant for sereneness, to send up mild white vapors among mild white hairs, not among torn iron-grey locks like mine." He knows what peace looks like and knows he's not eligible for it.

Then the fire hissing in the waves and the ship shooting past "the bubble the sinking pipe made." That's the whole tragedy in one image: something that could have comforted him, extinguished by his own hand, and the ship already gone by. Stubb kept a whole rack of pipes to disinfect the air of mortality. Ahab throws his one away. That's the difference between them, and it's a difference of about two pages.

annotations.quote: For a Khan of the plank, and a king of the sea, and a great lord of Leviathans was Ahab.
annotations.note: The narwhale-tusk throne makes him a sea-king in the Norse line, and Melville means it. The book is going to insist that a whaleman can be royalty, and this is the coronation—right before he throws away the one thing that eased him.

annotations.quote: as if, like the dying whale, my final jets were the strongest and fullest of trouble.
annotations.note: Ahab compares his own smoke to the death-spout of a whale, and doesn't hear what he's said. He's already identifying with the hunted thing's death. The hunter and the prey keep collapsing into each other in this book.

annotations.quote: This thing that is meant for sereneness, to send up mild white vapors among mild white hairs, not among torn iron-grey locks like mine.
annotations.note: He knows exactly what serenity is for and rules himself out of it. The most self-aware line Ahab speaks before the quarter-deck, and it's about a pipe.

annotations.quote: The fire hissed in the waves; the same instant the ship shot by the bubble the sinking pipe made.
annotations.note: Comfort discarded, and the ship past it before it's sunk. Melville does a whole tragedy in a sentence about a bubble. Stubb keeps a rack of pipes; Ahab throws his only one into the sea. That's the two men in one gesture.

links.why: The scene with Stubb that leaves Ahab on the stool with the pipe.
Ahab's next soliloquy: what he renounces serenity for.

links.q: look not too long in the face of the fire
links.why: Ishmael's own warning about staring into fire.
